title: Chapter 89 — Fast-Fish and Loose-Fish
paragraphs: The mention of the waif and waif-poles in the chapter before last calls for some account of the laws and regulations of the whale fishery, of which the waif may be considered the grand symbol and badge.

It frequently happens that when several ships are cruising together, a whale may be struck by one vessel, then escape, and finally be killed and captured by another. And within this general situation are many minor variations, all sharing this one feature. For example: after a weary and perilous chase and capture of a whale, the body may break loose from the ship in a violent storm and drift far to leeward, only to be retaken by a second whaler who, in a calm, snugly tows it alongside without risk of life or line. Thus the most maddening and violent disputes would often arise between fishermen, were there not some written or unwritten, universal, undisputed law applicable to all cases.

Perhaps the only formal whaling code ever enacted by a legislature was Holland's, decreed by the States-General in A.D. 1695. But although no other nation has ever had a written whaling law, American fishermen have acted as their own lawmakers and lawyers in this matter. They have devised a system that for concise completeness outdoes Justinian's Pandects and the By-laws of the Chinese Society for the Suppression of Meddling with other People's Business. Yes, these laws are so short they could be engraved on a Queen Anne's farthing, or on the barb of a harpoon, and worn around the neck.
I. A Fast-Fish belongs to the party fast to it.
II. A Loose-Fish is fair game for anybody who can soonest catch it.
But what causes trouble with this masterful code is the admirable brevity of it, which requires a vast volume of commentary to explain it.

First: What is a Fast-Fish? Alive or dead, a fish is technically fast when it is connected with an occupied ship or boat by any medium at all controllable by the occupant or occupants — a mast, an oar, a nine-inch cable, a telegraph wire, or a strand of cobweb, it is all the same. Likewise, a fish is technically fast when it bears a waif or any other recognized symbol of possession, so long as the party waifing it plainly shows both its ability to take the fish alongside at any time, and its intention to do so.

These are the learned commentaries. But the commentaries of the whalemen themselves sometimes consist of hard words and harder knocks — the Coke-upon-Littleton (the standard English law textbook) of the fist. True, among the more upright and honorable whalemen, allowances are always made for special cases where it would be an outrageous moral injustice for one party to claim possession of a whale previously chased or killed by another. But others are by no means so scrupulous.

Some fifty years ago there was a curious case of whale-trover (a suit to recover the value of goods wrongfully taken) litigated in England. The plaintiffs stated that after a hard chase of a whale in the northern seas, and when indeed they (the plaintiffs) had succeeded in harpooning the fish, they were at last, through peril of their lives, obliged to abandon not only their lines but their boat itself. Eventually the defendants — the crew of another ship — came up with the whale, struck, killed, seized, and finally appropriated it before the very eyes of the plaintiffs. And when those defendants were confronted, their captain snapped his fingers in the plaintiffs' faces and assured them that by way of a doxology (a closing hymn of praise) to the deed he had done, he would now retain their line, harpoons, and boat, which had remained attached to the whale at the time of the seizure. So the plaintiffs sued for the recovery of the value of their whale, line, harpoons, and boat.

Mr. Erskine represented the defendants; Lord Ellenborough was the judge. In the course of the defense, the witty Erskine illustrated his point by referring to a recent crim. con. case (a suit for adultery), in which a gentleman had tried in vain to curb his wife's vicious ways and had finally abandoned her on the seas of life; but years later, regretting that step, he sued to get her back. Erskine had been on the other side, and he had argued then that although the gentleman had originally harpooned the lady, and once had her fast, and had only abandoned her at last because of the terrible strain of her plunging viciousness, abandon her he nevertheless did, so that she became a loose-fish; and therefore when a later gentleman harpooned her again, the lady became that later gentleman's property, together with any harpoon that might be found sticking in her.
Now in the present case, Erskine argued that the whale and the lady each served to illustrate the other.

These arguments and counter-arguments being duly heard, the very learned judge officially decided as follows: As for the boat, he awarded it to the plaintiffs, because they had merely abandoned it to save their lives. But with regard to the disputed whale, harpoons, and line, they belonged to the defendants — the whale because it was a Loose-Fish at the time of the final capture, and the harpoons and line because when the fish made off with them, it (the fish) acquired property in those articles, and hence anybody who afterward took the fish had a right to them. Now the defendants afterward took the fish; therefore, the aforesaid articles were theirs.

An ordinary man looking at this decision of the very learned judge might possibly object to it. But plowed down to the bedrock of the matter, the two great principles laid down in the twin whaling laws previously quoted — applied and explained by Lord Ellenborough in the above-cited case — these two laws touching Fast-Fish and Loose-Fish will, on reflection, be found the fundamentals of all human law. For notwithstanding its complicated decorative sculpture, the Temple of the Law, like the Temple of the Philistines, has but two pillars to stand on.

Is it not a saying on everyone's lips that possession is half the law — regardless of how the thing came into possession? But often possession is the whole of the law. What are the bodies and souls of Russian serfs and Republican slaves but Fast-Fish, of which possession is the whole of the law? What to the greedy landlord is the widow's last mite but a Fast-Fish? What is yonder undetected villain's marble mansion with a door-plate for a waif — what is that but a Fast-Fish? What is the ruinous discount that Mordecai the broker gets from poor Woebegone the bankrupt, on a loan to keep Woebegone's family from starving — what is that ruinous discount but a Fast-Fish? What is the Archbishop of Savesoul's income of £100,000, seized from the meager bread and cheese of hundreds of thousands of broken-backed laborers, all sure of heaven without any of Savesoul's help — what is that globular £100,000 but a Fast-Fish? What are the Duke of Dunder's hereditary towns and hamlets but Fast-Fish? What to that mighty harpooner John Bull is poor Ireland but a Fast-Fish? What to that apostolic lancer Brother Jonathan (the United States) is Texas but a Fast-Fish? And concerning all these, is not Possession the whole of the law?
But if the doctrine of Fast-Fish applies fairly generally, the related doctrine of Loose-Fish applies more widely still. It holds everywhere, internationally and universally.

What was America in 1492 but a Loose-Fish, in which Columbus planted the Spanish standard by way of waifing it (flagging it as claimed) for his royal master and mistress? What was Poland to the Czar? What was Greece to the Turk? What was India to England? And what will Mexico finally be to the United States? Loose-Fish, all of them.

What are the Rights of Man and the Liberties of the World but Loose-Fish? What are all men's minds and opinions but Loose-Fish? What is the principle of religious belief in them but a Loose-Fish? To the showy, smuggling wordmongers, what are the thoughts of thinkers but Loose-Fish? What is the great globe itself but a Loose-Fish? And what are you, reader, but a Loose-Fish — and a Fast-Fish, too?
